meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Good management consists of showing average people how to do the work of superior people'?
meta.ogDescription: Rockefeller died in 1937. The earliest located appearance of such remarks is a 1958 address by Jim Low, twenty-one years later. No primary source has been located.

answer.label: No source in Rockefeller’s lifetime — attribution unverified
answer.authorDates: Credited to John D. Rockefeller (1839–1937) · earliest located appearance of such remarks: 1958
answer.sourceLine: No speech, letter, interview or book of Rockefeller’s has ever been produced for this line, and his only memoir, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), contains neither “average people” nor “superior people.” Wikiquote files the quotation under Disputed, citing for the Rockefeller credit only The Harper Book of Quotations (1993) and noting that the earliest published occurrence of such remarks yet located is a 1958 conference address by Jim Low — twenty-one years after Rockefeller’s death.

source.excerpt: Good management consists of showing average people how to do the work of superior people.
trail: 1909 — Rockefeller publishes his only memoir, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events. A search of the full text turns up no passage about average people doing the work of superior people, and neither phrase appears in it (Project Gutenberg ↗).
23 May 1937 — Rockefeller dies at Ormond Beach, Florida, aged 97, having spent his last decades on philanthropy (Wikipedia ↗). Nothing resembling this line has been traced to his lifetime.

October 1958 — the earliest published occurrence of such remarks yet located is Jim Low’s “The Human in Public Relations,” an address printed in Proceedings, Seventh Annual Meeting of the Agricultural Research Institute, October 13–14, 1958, Washington, Pt. 3, p. 83 — twenty-one years after Rockefeller’s death (Wikiquote, Disputed ↗).

Today — quote sites print it as Rockefeller’s with no primary source. LibQuotes gives the variant wording “consists in showing” and cites The Forbes Scrapbook of Thoughts on the Business of Life (1950) — a business-quotation compilation, not anything Rockefeller wrote or said (LibQuotes ↗).
source.excerptNote: There is no original context to show. This is the line as it appears in modern quotation collections — no speech, letter, interview or manuscript of Rockefeller’s has ever been produced for it, and his own 1909 memoir does not contain it (Project Gutenberg ↗).

source.rightsNote: The wording cannot be tied to any work by Rockefeller, so no public-domain claim can be made for it. The earliest text known to carry such remarks — a 1958 conference proceedings — falls well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, and the compilations that attach the line to Rockefeller (The Harper Book of Quotations, 1993; the Forbes Scrapbook editions) are themselves modern, in-copyright books. Status: uncertain.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.heading: About John D. Rockefeller
author.metaLine: 1839–1937 · American oil magnate and philanthropist, founder of Standard Oil
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller Sr. (8 July 1839 – 23 May 1937) started out as a sixteen-year-old bookkeeper and founded Standard Oil in 1870, building a company that controlled roughly ninety per cent of US oil production by 1900 before the Supreme Court broke it up in 1911. He spent his later decades giving the money away, founding the University of Chicago and what became Rockefeller University. He left remarkably little quotable prose: his one memoir, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), is short and guarded and contains nothing like this line — part of why so many invented maxims have managed to attach themselves to his name.

misattribution.heading: How a management-training line ended up on an oil baron
misattribution.intro: Rockefeller is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: any crisp sentence about money, work or organisation can be pinned to him and sound right. This one has the shape of a mid-century management maxim, and the paper trail runs backwards through quotation compilations rather than forwards from anything he said.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line in its Disputed section, giving the Rockefeller credit only as it appears in The Harper Book of Quotations (1993) by Robert I. Fitzhenry, p. 71, and noting that the earliest published occurrence of such remarks yet located came from Jim Low in 1958 (Wikiquote ↗).

Every citation on offer is a compendium. LibQuotes points to The Forbes Scrapbook of Thoughts on the Business of Life (1950) (LibQuotes ↗); the Internet Archive’s scanned copies of that title are later editions, so that particular citation could not be checked here. Neither it nor the 1993 Harper book reproduces a speech, letter or page of Rockefeller’s.

The form that circulates most is “consists of showing,” but compilations also print “consists in showing” — the kind of drift you get with a line that has no fixed original text to check against (LibQuotes ↗).
A “leadership” rewrite of the same sentence circulates under Rockefeller’s name with no source of any kind attached (The Socratic Method ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: nobody has shown that Rockefeller said or wrote this. The earliest text anyone has located carrying such remarks is a 1958 conference address by Jim Low, and the earliest Rockefeller credit we could verify is The Harper Book of Quotations (1993) — LibQuotes points to a 1950 Forbes compilation, which we could not check, since the Internet Archive scan is a 1984 edition. So the sentiment may well be a mid-century management idea that later acquired a famous name (Wikiquote, Disputed ↗).

context.heading: Why it sticks to him anyway
lead: Rockefeller really was the era’s great organiser — Standard Oil, founded in 1870, controlled roughly ninety per cent of American oil production by 1900, until the Supreme Court ordered its breakup in 1911 (Wikipedia ↗). A maxim about getting extraordinary output from ordinary staff sounds exactly like something the man who built that machine would say, which is precisely why it survives without evidence.

But read the sentence again and it is pure management-seminar vocabulary: “good management consists of…” is how a training handout opens, not how a Gilded Age industrialist wrote. That is an impression, not proof — the documented facts are simply that the earliest located appearance of such remarks is a 1958 address, and the earliest Rockefeller credit we could verify is a 1993 quotation book — LibQuotes cites a 1950 Forbes compilation we could not check.
context.pull: The trail runs backwards through quotation books, not forwards from anything he said.
